name: Ivatan
confidence_why: Cottle & Cottle 1958, Reid 1966 and Gallego 2022 all put stress on the final syllable in the great majority of Ivatan words, but all three also record words with contrastive penultimate stress (Cottle's tiban 'look' vs tsíban 'accompany', Gallego's native talón vs Ilokano-loan tálon), so the language has a final-stress default with lexical exceptions rather than a strictly fixed final stress.
catalog_quote: Acute accent is only used to indicate stress on other than ultimate syllables. Words without an acute accent have ultimate syllable stress. The Cottles considered length to be phonemic. The orthography used in this dissertation however is based on the assumption that phonetic length is indicative of either (1) geminate consonants or vowels, or (2) a feature of stress in certain environments. audit.recode_to: final (ultimate) default stress with lexically specified non-final exceptions, stress phonemic - i.e. drop counts as exceptionless (the strict set) (fixed-strict -> fixed: final syllable-with-lexical-exceptions / 'predominantly final, contrastive'); keep dom=final. Cite Cottle & Cottle 1958:32 sec. 4.5 as deciding source, Reid 1966:4 fn.9 (stress listed as a phoneme; acute marks non-final stress) as corroboration.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both Reid 1966 passages are verbatim in the extracted text we hold (p.4 fn.9, lines 245-247; p.145, lines 4854-4857). (2) But the record over-reads them: Reid's footnote is a spelling convention ('words without an acute accent have ultimate stress') and the same footnote lists stress among the Central Ivatan phonemes; p.145 speaks of 'verb stems having ultimate stress', implying others do not. The source Reid relies on, Cottle & Cottle 1958 (downloaded now from the Rosetta Project scan, p.32 sec. 4.5, page scan read), says stress 'is believed to be a significant feature', falls on the last syllable 'for the vast majority of words', and gives non-final items with (near-)minimal pairs (mangamong / mangámong, tiban / tsíban, dekey vs mákey). Gallego 2022 (downloaded, ANU open thesis) shows the Babuyan dialect likewise has stress-only contrasts (babáng vs bábang etc., native vs establish
audit.second_reader_evidence: Quote check (copies we hold: the deciding quote is verbatim at the text (= Reid 1966 p.4, continuation of fn.9): 'Acute accent is only used to indicate stress on other than ultimate syllables. Words without an acute accent have ultimate syllable stress. The Cottles considered length to be phonemic..'. I confirm the compilers key observation: the immediately preceding lines of the same footnote (txt 241-244) list 'The phonemes of Central Ivatan.. h, l, r, s, v, w, y, ' (stress).' - Reid treats stress as a phoneme, and the quoted sentence is an orthographic convention, not a fixed-stress claim. sources.citation: Gallego, Maria Kristina S. 2022. The stratigraphy of a community: 150 years of language contact and change in Babuyan Claro, Philippines. PhD thesis, Australian National University. hdl.handle.net/1885/275585
sources.quote: No stress rule stated (Appendix A gives only segment inventories). Table 32 shows Ibatan (Babuyan dialect) word pairs 'only differing in terms of stress placement': native babáng 'carry on the back' vs Ilokano-loan bábang 'hesitate', barót/bárot, sagót/ságot, talón/tálon - native stems final-stressed, established loans penult-stressed, i.e. surface-contrastive stress in the present-day lexicon.
sources.locator: pp.128-129, Table 32 'Pairs of near homophonous native and non-native forms in Ibatan'; Appendix A p.237-238 (phoneme inventory after Maree 2007:19)
sources.note: Only recent open work on the Babuyan dialect; Table 32 documents stress-only contrasts (native final vs Ilokano-loan penult).

sources.citation: Cottle, Morris & Shirley Cottle. 1958. The significant sounds of Ivatan. In: Studies in Philippine Linguistics by members of the Summer Institute of Linguistics (Pacific Branch), Oceania Linguistic Monographs 3, pp. 24-33. Sydney: University of Sydney. (Rosetta Project scan, archive.org item rosettaproject_ivv_phon-1 + _detail-1)
sources.quote: 'Stress is believed to be a significant feature in these dialects. For the vast majority of words stress falls on the last syllable and it is convenient and adequate if such words receive no accent mark. For the remaining words, stress on non-final syllables should be indicated by means of an acute accent mark.' Examples: tiban 'look' / tsíban 'accompany'; mangamong 'taking fish from net' / mangámong 'general term for fishing'; takey 'field', dekey 'small' / mákey 'like'. 4.4: long vs short consonants and vowels contrast (rakoh 'large' / rakkoh 'largest', pa 'also' / paa 'thigh').
sources.locator: p.32, section 4.5 'Stress' (PDF page 8); also 4.4 'Length' same page
sources.note: Primary phonemic study underlying Reid's footnote; p.32 states stress is 'significant', majority-final, with non-final lexical items and (near-)minimal pairs.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid record ibat1238 (glottolog.org/resource/languoid/id/) and iso/ivv
sources.quote: Identity only: ibat1238 'Ibatan' [ivb] has dialects Babuyan [babu1242], Basco Ivatan [basc1238], Southern Ivatan [sout2903]; ISO ivv is assigned to Itbayat [ivat1242]. Reid 1966 (Basco/Central Ivatan) and Cottle 1958 (Southern + Northern=Basco Ivatan) therefore fall inside ibat1238; no languoid mismatch.

sources.quote: 'As a guide to proper pronunciation, accent marks are used to indicate which syllable or syllables are to be stressed. An acute accent is used to mark the strongest stress in the word while the circumflex accent is used when the final syllable is stressed and at the same time has a glottal stop.' Stress is marked word by word; no positional rule given (pedagogical).

tone.quote: Suprasegmental features are also analyzed. It has been observed that stress, typically characterized by pitch, intensity, and length, is significant in the Batanic microgroup. Its phonemic status as a suprasegmental phoneme is established by means of minimal pairs. [...] 3.7.3. Stress. Stress is phonemic in Ibatan, as attested by the minimal pair shown below (Maree, 2007, p. 20). Penultima [ˈbaːro] 'feather palm' Ultima [baˈro] 'young man'
tone.locator: p.41 (ch.3 introduction) and p.68 section 3.7.3 'Stress' (Ibatan); parallel sections 3.5.3 p.60 (Ivasay) and 3.6.3 p.64 (Isamorong); summary p.71 ('Stress is also phonemic in these languages')
tone.summary: No tone; lexical stress (cued by pitch, intensity, length) contrasting penult vs final position in Ivasay, Isamorong and Babuyan Ibatan.

tone.quote: The accent system—suprasegmental phoneme—is observed in many of the Philippine languages and its primary feature is length, which is realized by the prolongation or shortening of the penultimate syllable. [...] The languages in the group vary from each other as to the accent system, though all the languages have lost the Proto-Philippine accent; Itbayat and Yami do not possess the system, Ivatan and Babuyan Claro, on the other hand, do. The comparison of the words containing the duration accent in Ivatan and their cognates in Itbayat reveals that the disappearance of the consonant /h/ in Itbayat [...] results in the prolongation of the vowel before or after the consonant.
tone.locator: p.108, English summary; accent typology table and definition p.113 (fig.1, section IV(A)); Isamorong/Babuyan minimal pairs table 3 and sonagram discussion pp.114-118; conclusion p.123
tone.summary: No tone: word prosody analysed as a lexical durational accent (long vs short penultimate syllable) in Ivasay/Isamorong Ivatan and Babuyan Claro Ibatan; pitch examined instrumentally but not treated as distinctive.

sources.citation: Wolfenden, Elmer. 1972. Review of A Tagmemic Grammar of Ivatan, by Cesar A. Hidalgo and Araceli C. Hidalgo (LSP Special Monograph 2, Manila, 1971). Philippine Journal of Linguistics 3(2): 125-129.

tone.quote: Part I consists of Chapter Two, which is a description of the phonological component of the language. In this section, the phonemes and their allophones are described with reference to their distribution in syllables and word patterns. Suprasegmental phenomena of phonemic stress, vowel length, and intonation levels are discussed briefly. It is interesting to note that Southern Ivatan has both phonemic stress and phonemic vowel length in contradistinction to Northern Ivatan (Reid, 1966.3) which has only phonemic stress.
tone.locator: p.125 (first page of the review), paragraph on Part I / Chapter Two
tone.summary: No tone reported; suprasegmentals of Southern Ivatan per H&H 1971 = phonemic stress + phonemic vowel length + intonation levels.
